questions.prompt: In machine learning, a word embedding is best described as:
options: A dictionary mapping words to their definitions
A one-hot encoded binary vector
A fixed-length vector of real numbers representing a word
A probability distribution over the vocabulary
questions.explanation: An embedding is a dense, fixed-length vector of real numbers. Unlike one-hot encoding — which is sparse and enormous, one slot per vocabulary word — an embedding packs meaning into a few hundred numbers, and similar words end up with similar numbers.

questions.prompt: True or false: if two word vectors have a small Euclidean distance between them, the words probably have similar meanings.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: True. This is the founding principle of embedding spaces: semantic similarity is stored as geometric closeness. Similar things live near each other — that is the whole trick.

questions.prompt: BERT-base uses 768-dimensional embeddings. What does the 768 actually count?
options: The number of words in BERT's vocabulary
The number of components (individual numbers) in each word's vector
The number of layers in the model
The number of attention heads
questions.explanation: Dimension = how many numbers are in the list. Each word BERT-base knows is represented by 768 numbers. GPT-3 uses 12,288 — same idea, a longer list per word.

questions.prompt: Why can't a single number (a scalar) capture a word's full meaning?
options: Scalars can only hold positive values
Computers cannot store single numbers precisely enough
Scalars take up too much memory
A word has many attributes — gender, sentiment, category — and each needs its own dimension
questions.explanation: One number can encode one attribute. But "queen" is royal AND female AND human AND singular. You need many numbers — a vector — to hold all of those at once.
Add component by component: 1+4 = 5, −2+5 = 3, 3+(−1) = 2 → `[5, 3, 2]`. If you got `[-3, -7, 4]` you subtracted; `[4, -10, -3]` means you multiplied.
questions.hint: Line the two vectors up and add each matching pair.

questions.explanation: Multiply every component by 3: `[6, -3, 12]`. Note the −1 stays negative. Scaling changes the vector's length, never its direction — it points the same way, just longer.
questions.hint: Every component gets multiplied, not just the first.

questions.prompt: The famous word2vec result is vector(king) − vector(man) + vector(woman) ≈ vector(queen). Why does this work?
options: The model memorized this specific analogy during training
Directions in embedding space encode semantic relationships, so the "gender direction" transfers between words
"queen" happens to be the nearest neighbour of "king"
The two vectors differ in exactly one dimension
questions.explanation: Nothing memorized it. Subtracting man from king isolates a direction that means roughly "royalty minus maleness"; adding woman walks that same direction from a different starting point. Relationships live in directions, not positions.

questions.prompt: GPT-3 uses 12,288-dimensional embeddings rather than, say, 3-dimensional ones. What's the advantage?
options: More dimensions make the model run faster
Fewer dimensions would actually use more memory
There is no real advantage — the number is arbitrary
More dimensions give the model room to encode finer distinctions between words
questions.explanation: Each dimension is a slot for an attribute. Three slots forces the model to jam all of English into three numbers; 12,288 slots lets it separate "bank (river)" from "bank (money)". It's the difference between a 3-crayon box and a 12,288-crayon box.
Multiply matching components, then add: 2·4 + 3·(−1) + 1·5 = 8 − 3 + 5 = 10. If you got 16 you dropped the minus sign; 14 means you added the vectors first and then summed.
questions.hint: Multiply the pairs first, then add all three products — watch the negative.

questions.prompt: Given v = `[3, 4]`, compute its L2 norm ‖v‖
questions.explanation: ‖v‖ = √(3² + 4²) = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. The classic 3-4-5 triangle — the norm is just Pythagoras, extended to any number of dimensions. If you answered 25 you forgot the square root; 7 means you added the components.
questions.hint: Square each component, add, then take the square root.

questions.prompt: Two vectors have a dot product of 0. Geometrically, this means they are:
options: Parallel — pointing the same direction
Opposite — pointing in reverse directions
Orthogonal — perpendicular to each other
Equal in length
questions.explanation: Zero dot product means zero alignment: the vectors are perpendicular. In an embedding space, orthogonal directions carry independent information — one dimension can encode "is it an animal?" without disturbing another encoding sentiment.

questions.prompt: What does normalizing a vector do?
options: Sets every component to zero
Reverses the vector's direction
Doubles the vector's magnitude
Scales it to length 1 while preserving its direction
questions.explanation: Divide a vector by its own norm and you get a unit vector: same direction, length exactly 1. This is how you strip away "how big" and keep only "which way" — useful whenever you care about angle rather than magnitude.

questions.prompt: What is the unit vector (normalized form) of `[3, 4]`?
questions.explanation: The norm is 5, so divide each component by 5: `[3/5, 4/5]` = `[0.6, 0.8]`. Check it: 0.6² + 0.8² = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1 ✓. If you got `[0.43, 0.57]` you divided by 3+4 = 7; `[0.12, 0.16]` means you divided by 25.
questions.hint: Find the norm first, then divide every component by it.

questions.prompt: True or false: cosine similarity and the dot product always give the same result.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. They agree only when both vectors are already unit length. Otherwise the dot product also carries magnitude information, while cosine divides it out and reports direction alone. Cosine is a special case of the dot product, not a synonym for it.
1·1 + 1·(−1) = 1 − 1 = 0. Zero means orthogonal: one vector points northeast, the other southeast, and they're exactly 90° apart. Getting 2 means you ignored the minus sign.
questions.hint: The second components have opposite signs — that matters.

questions.prompt: What is the cosine similarity between `[1, 0]` and `[0, 1]`?
options: 1 — identical direction
0 — orthogonal
−1 — opposite direction
0.5 — partially similar
questions.explanation: Dot product = 1·0 + 0·1 = 0. Both norms are 1, so cosine = 0 / (1 · 1) = 0. These are the two axis directions — perpendicular, sharing no information at all.
questions.hint: Compute the dot product on top first; if it's zero, the whole fraction is zero.

questions.prompt: In a transformer's attention mechanism, the relevance score between a query and a key is computed as:
options: The Euclidean distance between them
The sum of their components
The dot product of the query and key vectors
The average of their magnitudes
questions.explanation: score = q · k, later divided by √d_k for scale. This is why the dot product is worth mastering: "how much should this token pay attention to that token" is answered by a single dot product, billions of times per forward pass.

questions.prompt: You compute dot products between a query word and three candidates: A = 12.5, B = −3.2, C = 0.1. Which candidate is most relevant to the query?
options: B — the largest absolute value indicates the strongest relationship
C — closest to zero means most neutral and therefore safest
You cannot tell without knowing the vector magnitudes
A — the highest positive score means the most alignment
questions.explanation: Higher dot product = more alignment = more relevant, so A wins. B's negative score means it points somewhat opposite to the query; C ≈ 0 means it's essentially unrelated. Attention would send almost all of its weight to A.
